newsitem.title: USA: NYCE cotton called to open flat to 0.10 weaker.
newsitem.headline: NYCE cotton called to open flat to 0.10 weaker.

text.p: NYCE cotton futures were called to open unchanged to 0.10 cent weaker Tuesday, based on market orders at 1017 EDT, dealers said.

The lower call comes despite the release this morning of a constructive spec/hedge report. The data showed an increase in the net speculative short positions to 22.8 percent from 19.5 percent a week ago.
"The spec/hedge shows funds to be a little bit shorter," said one trader. "Yesterday they covered quite a bit, but they could still cover some more."
Additionally, ongoing planting delays were viewed as supportive, they said.

USDA's planting progress report released late Monday showed planting continues to run behind last year. USDA reported 44 percent of the crop was planted, compared with 51 percent in the same period a year ago and the five-year average of 51 percent.
But some traders said the market's upside potential was limited, with ideal growing conditions in West Texas weighing on sentiment.

"The moisture situation in West Texas is so bearish, any rallies are going to be short-lived," said one Lubbock, Texas-based trader. "It is the best moisture situation for this time of year on record."

Monday, most-active July cotton ended 0.67 cent higher at 72.65 cents per lb after trading from 72.00 to 73.35 cents, its highest level since hitting 73.75 cents on April 30. New-crop December finished 0.35 firmer at 74.67 cents.
While analysts initially viewed Monday's USDA report as neutral, they said it may have fuelled Monday's rally by indicating some tightness in world supplies.
USDA raised U.S. ending stocks to 4.25 million bales from 4.05 million bales this season, and lowered world stocks by 1 million bales, to 36.54 million bales in 1997/98.
World consumption, meanwhile, rose to 88.5 million bales, from 86.44 million bales this year. The higher use estimate contributed to the decline in stocks.
In the U.S., production was estimated at 18.50 million 480-lb bales, exports at 7.3 million bales, and domestic use at 11.0 million bales.
USDA's final estimates for 1996/97 put output at 18.9 million bales, the third largest crop on record. Yields averaged 707 lbs per harvested acre, the second highest yield on record, USDA said.
On the charts, traders Support remained at the contract low of 71.00 cents basis July, followed by 70.00 cents.
